basketball-shorts.h2: The half of the uniform nobody specifies
intro: Teams spend an hour choosing a jersey and thirty seconds choosing the shorts that go with it. Then in December they discover the two blues do not match, the inseam is wrong for half the roster, and the waistband has stopped holding.

Shorts fail more often than jerseys do, and almost always for reasons decided at order time rather than on the court. They also take abrasion a jersey never sees — every time a player sits, slides or takes a charge, concentrated on a small area of fabric.
This page is about the four decisions that actually matter, and none of them is the color.
basketball-shorts.faqH2: Shorts questions we get every season

faqs.q: Why do our shorts not quite match our jerseys?
faqs.a: Because they are different fabrics. A jersey knit and a shorts fabric take dye at slightly different rates, so the same specification lands a shade apart on each. On navy it is invisible; on a saturated color it shows in every photograph. Ordering both on one job from one production run is what prevents it.

faqs.q: Can we have pockets?
faqs.a: On practice and training shorts, yes, and they earn their place — nobody is being fouled hard in a shooting drill. On game shorts most leagues do not permit them, and there is a sound argument against them anyway: a pocket is somewhere a finger catches during contact. Check your league's wording before deciding.

faqs.q: What inseam should we order?
faqs.a: Whatever your players prefer, cut proportionally within each size. Longer shorts ride less during lateral movement; shorter ones move more freely. On a training pair there is no reason the whole squad has to wear the same length — offering two costs nothing and produces a set people actually wear.

faqs.q: Lined or unlined?
faqs.a: A liner adds opacity, means the shorts can be worn on their own, and adds warmth — which in a Florida gym is a real cost. Unlined is cooler and assumes compression underneath, which most players at high school level and above wear. Ask the roster; it is a genuine preference and easy to collect on a sizing form.

faqs.q: How many spares should we order?
faqs.a: More than for jerseys. Shorts come off in the gym and go into a bag that may not be the right bag, and across a season a squad of fifteen will typically lose three or four pairs. Two or three spares in the middle sizes costs very little and saves a mid-season reorder.

blocks.h3: Four decisions, in the order they matter

rows.p: A game pair, a practice pair and a training pair are three different specifications, and buying one for all three is the most common and most expensive mistake. Game shorts are built to a league's rules and a set's look; practice shorts take four times the wear and are better with pockets; training shorts are worn to the gym and back and want comfort over compliance.

Players routinely take one size on top and another below. A broad-shouldered guard with a narrow waist is a large jersey and a medium short, and the reverse is just as common. Ordering both from one size letter guarantees returns on any roster above about ten.

The same inseam sits at completely different points on a five-foot-four guard and a six-foot-eight center. Cut proportionally within each size it looks intentional across a roster; cut to one number it is halfway up one player's thigh and at another's knee.

rows.h: The waistband, which is where they fail
rows.p: A double-stitched band with wider elastic holds its recovery far longer than a single-stitched narrow one, and a flat drawcord outlasts a round one at the eyelet where fraying starts. This is the part that retires a pair, not the fabric.

blocks.close: If you are ordering a full set, order the shorts and the jersey on one job even where the budget only stretches to one this season — we can produce the jersey now and hold the shorts specification, so next year's shorts match this year's jersey exactly rather than approximately. How a full set is put together covers what that looks like.

blocks.h3: What a shorts order should include
items: Two pairs per player for practice. One means the second session of the week is in a damp pair. Practice shorts are the cheapest item on any kit list and the most frequently under-ordered.
Spares in the middle sizes. Shorts are the garment most likely to leave the gym in somebody else's bag. Two or three spares cost less than the mid-season reorder they replace.
A number inside the waistband. Small, printed, invisible when worn. A locker room full of identical black shorts is the definition of an item that goes missing, and this cuts the losses for no cost.
Waist measurements, collected separately. Not inferred from the jersey sheet. Fifteen seconds per player, and it is not a number anyone volunteers.
A different color for practice. It stops the game shorts being quietly absorbed into daily training use, which is the most common way a game set is destroyed a year early.

callout.cap: The one that costs most to skip
callout.p: Waist measurements. Players routinely take one size on top and another below, and a set ordered from jersey sizes alone will generate exchanges on any roster above about ten. Fifteen seconds per player, collected on the same form as everything else.

basketball-shirts.eyebrow: Team shirts, base layers and training tops
basketball-shirts.h2: When a shirt is the right garment and a jersey is not
intro: A jersey is worn during games. A shirt is worn everywhere else — to sessions, at sessions, home from sessions, to school, on a bus, and around a tournament venue between games.
That makes a team shirt the most-seen garment a program owns, by a wide margin, and it is usually the one specified in ten seconds as an afterthought to the kit order.
The decision that matters here is not fabric or fit. It is which of two jobs the shirt is being bought to do, because they want different garments.

faqs.q: Should the shirt match the game jersey exactly?
faqs.a: It does not have to, and there is an argument that it should not. A shirt in the program's colors with the program's name reads as team wear; one that is a copy of the jersey without numbers reads as an incomplete jersey. What it should share is the color family, which means ordering it on the same job so the shades match.

faqs.q: Numbers on a team shirt?
faqs.a: No, in almost every case. A number dates the garment to one roster, stops it being handed on, and serves no function outside a game. The program's name does the work you are actually buying.

faqs.q: Long sleeve or short?
faqs.a: Short for most Florida programs, because the buildings are warm more often than they are cold. A long sleeve earns its place for travel days and over-air-conditioned venues, and it is worth having as a second item rather than instead of the short-sleeve one.

faqs.q: Can we sell these to parents?
faqs.a: Many programs do, and it is worth deciding before the order rather than after. A run sized only to the squad cannot cover it, and a second run later carries its own setup — which costs more than over-ordering the first one by a comfortable margin.

faqs.q: How many per player?
faqs.a: One is the minimum and two is better, because a shirt worn to school on Monday is not available for the bus on Tuesday. Order spares beyond the roster as well: coaches, managers and volunteers all wear them, and a new player should have one on their first day rather than in week four.

blocks.h3: Two jobs, and they pull apart

items: Conditioning, warm-ups, summer sessions and any facility that is not properly air conditioned.
Judge the knit openness rather than the wicking claim — everything wicks, and in humid air evaporation is slow, so airflow is what actually cools.
Fit closer, because a loose technical shirt flaps during drills.
Two per player, because one means the second session is in a damp shirt.
Accept that it reads as sportswear and will mostly be worn at the gym.
School corridors, bus journeys, tournament venues, and anywhere a player is seen not playing.
Comfort decides whether it gets worn at all — an unpleasant shirt is worn to training and taken off immediately after.
Cut it looser and longer than a game jersey. A close fit limits when players reach for it.
Put the program's name on it at a size a jersey could never carry, and leave numbers off.
Order a wider size range than the roster if families might want them.

blocks.close: Where a program genuinely needs both, two different shirts is cheaper than most people expect and better than one compromise — they are among the least expensive items on any kit list. Programs deciding between a shirt and a sleeveless top for training will find the trade set out under what a tank does differently.

steps.p: Worn at sessions points at technical fabric; worn around the program points at a softer hand. If both, order two different shirts rather than one compromise.

steps.h: Put the program's name on it
steps.p: At a size a jersey could not carry, because the number takes priority there and here nothing does. This is the recognition you are paying for.

steps.h: Cut it looser than the jersey
steps.p: And size it separately. Players who take a medium jersey frequently want a large shirt, and ordering both from one letter produces a set half the roster does not wear.
Beyond the roster, in both directions, if coaches, staff or families might want one. A second run later carries its own setup.

steps.h: Order it with the rest of the kit
steps.p: So the colors match the jerseys and the setup is paid once rather than twice.

practice-jerseys.h2: The kit that is worn four times more often and looked at far less
intro: A game jersey is worn twice a week in front of an audience. A practice jersey is worn four or five times a week in front of nobody, thrown in a bag damp, and washed in whatever is available.

It is a different garment doing a different job, and specifying it as a cheaper version of the game set gets it wrong in both directions — too much money on appearance nobody sees, too little on the durability doing all the work.
It is also the cheapest insurance a uniform budget can buy, because a game set absorbing four days a week of drill work is worn out in one season instead of three.

sides.h: Worn four or five times a week
items: Durability over breathability. This garment is going to lose; buy the fabric that loses slowly.
Two contrasting colors across the squad, so scrimmages split without pinnies.
Numbers only if the coach calls players by number, and never player names.
Dark or mid-tone colors. Court dirt is what retires practice kit, and it shows on light fabric within weeks.
Two or three per player, because the frequency is not comparable to a game set.

sides.h: Worn twice a week, in front of a crowd
items: Appearance matters — this is the jersey in the team photograph and on the court.
Full team identity: name, mark, numbers, the whole specification.
Player names if the program replaces kit annually rather than reissuing it.
Any color the program wants, because it is not being worn on the floor five days a week.
One set, or two if the division produces regular color clashes.

blocks.h3: What actually retires a practice jersey
blocks.lead: Not the fabric wearing through. Practice kit is almost always retired for one of these instead, which is what the specification should be built against.
items: Stretched bindings. Repeated pulling on and off takes the neckline and armholes past their recovery long before the body thins.
Ground-in floor dirt. Court sealant and rubber transfer onto light fabric and set with heat. A light gray practice jersey is unrecoverable by February.
Color drift between the two sides. Two practice colors that fade at different rates stop being distinguishable, which defeats the reason they exist.
Loss. Practice kit lives in bags, and bags get mixed up. This is what spares are for.
Being outgrown, in a youth program, which is entirely predictable and is why a practice set should be ordered across a size range rather than to one roster.

callout.p: A reversible practice jersey solves the scrimmage split with one garment per player rather than two. The trade is that two bonded layers are warmer, which in a Florida gym is a real cost rather than a technicality — and the per-unit price is higher, so the saving is smaller than the halved count suggests.

practice-jerseys.close: If a budget will not stretch to both a full game set and practice kit, the honest advice is to simplify the game set and keep the practice jerseys. The game set is what the practice kit is protecting, and why the two are specified differently sets out what each one is actually for.

faqs.q: How many practice jerseys per player?
faqs.a: Two at minimum, three for a squad practicing five or six days a week. One means it is worn Monday, worn damp Tuesday, and worn stiff Wednesday — which is the complaint parents and players raise most often about practice kit.

faqs.q: Do practice jerseys need numbers?
faqs.a: It depends on how you run a session. A coach working with eighteen players across a full court wants numbers and they save real time. With twelve players a coach knows every face, and skipping numbers lowers the cost noticeably across a full set.

faqs.q: Should practice kit match the game set?
faqs.a: In color family, usually yes. Exactly, rarely — the practice set fades and wears at a different rate, so a set that matched in November will not by March. Several programs deliberately use a different color so it is obvious which set a player has grabbed on a game day.

faqs.q: Two colors or reversibles?
faqs.a: Two colors in a warm gym, reversibles in a cool one. A reversible is two layers bonded together and is noticeably warmer; where the hall is properly air conditioned that costs nothing and the convenience is free, and where it is not, players notice within a session.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to order practice and game kit together?
faqs.a: Yes, noticeably. The setup and the color matching happen once across both rather than twice, and the two sets arrive together rather than one of them being chased in November.

basketball-tank-tops.eyebrow: Tanks, training tops and sleeveless kit
basketball-tank-tops.h2: The fewest parts a top can have
intro: A tank has no sleeves, no placket and nothing across the shoulder. That is the whole design, and every advantage and limitation follows from it.

It is the coolest garment we make, which in a Florida gym is not a marginal consideration. It has the fewest failure points, which matters for a set being handed down. And it leaves the shoulder joint entirely unobstructed, which is the joint basketball's two defining actions both rotate through.
What varies between a good tank and a poor one is not the fabric. It is where the armhole is cut and how the edges are finished.

blocks.h3: The decisions that actually change the garment

items.h: How deep should the armhole be?
p: Cut too shallow and it catches at the top of an overhead reach; too deep and it gapes at the side, which is uncomfortable in contact and shows more than most players want.

The right answer sits in a narrow band and has to move with the size — a youth medium and an adult double-extra-large do not want the same drop, which is why a run scaled linearly fits badly at both ends.

A bound edge — fabric folded over the raw edge and stitched — is more durable and slightly firmer, and it is the standard on a game garment. A raw or coverstitched edge is lighter and softer and is used on training kit.
The bindings are also the first place a tank fails, because they take more handling than any other part of it. On a set being reissued, that is worth paying attention to.

A high proportion of players wear a compression shirt under a tank. It changes the effective chest measurement slightly and the opacity requirement considerably — a light tank over a dark layer shows the outline of it.
One line on the sizing form settles it, and it removes an entire category of complaint.

A game tank has to satisfy an association's rules on number size and placement. A training tank does not, which means it can be cut deeper at the armhole and carry the program's name at a size a jersey could never accommodate.
Most programs that own one end up wanting the other, because the two are genuinely different purchases.

blocks.h3: Where a tank is the right answer
items: Game kit in a warm gym. The coolest option available and the standard cut in the sport for that reason.
Training and conditioning. Worn hard, washed often, and nobody reading anything off it.
Under a warm-up. No sleeves means no bunching under a second layer.
Camps and clinics. The cheapest identifiable garment a program can hand somebody for a week.
Summer and open-gym play, where a numbered game jersey would be wrong and a t-shirt would be too warm.

callout.p: A player who is broad across the shoulders relative to their chest will feel a tank at the armhole before anywhere else. Those are the players to size up, and they are usually obvious on a roster without measuring.

basketball-tank-tops.close: A tank is also the cheapest garment on any kit list to over-order, because it uses less fabric than any other top and takes the same setup. Ordering four more than the roster needs covers new players, replacements and staff for very little — and it is worth ordering across a wider size range than this season's squad, since a training set outlives the roster it was bought for.

faqs.q: Is a tank cooler than a sleeved jersey?
faqs.a: Yes, and in a Florida gym it is a noticeable difference rather than a technical one. A sleeve traps air against the upper arm and adds fabric across the shoulder, both of which a warm hall makes obvious within a quarter.

faqs.q: Do leagues allow sleeveless jerseys?
faqs.a: Almost all do — it is the standard cut in basketball. Some school associations have specific requirements about numbering and neckline rather than about sleeves, and those are worth checking against the rule book rather than against memory.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a game tank and a training tank?
faqs.a: The rules. A game tank is built around an association's requirements for number size and placement; a training tank has none of those, so it can be cut deeper at the armhole, narrower at the strap, and carry the program's name across the whole front.

faqs.q: How should we size them?
faqs.a: From the chest measurement, with anyone broad at the shoulder sized up. Also ask who wears a compression layer underneath — it affects both the size and the fabric weight you should choose.

faqs.q: Can we mix tanks and sleeved jerseys in one order?
faqs.a: Yes, and the fabric, color and decoration are identical across both, so a mixed set reads as one uniform on court. Note the preference against each player's name and the order is built that way.

colored-jerseys-uniforms.h2: The color is the identity, so choose it like one
intro: On a court at forty feet, the color is what identifies a team. Panel details, piping and tonal design elements all disappear at that distance; the base color and the number contrast are what remain.
That makes it the most consequential decision on a uniform order and the one most often made from a screen, in a room, against nothing in particular.

Two things go wrong. The color that arrives is not the one on the monitor, because a screen and a dye do not have the same range. And the color that arrives is the same as three other teams in the division, because nobody checked.

blocks.h3: Where a screen and a dye disagree
blocks.caption: A monitor makes color by emitting light and fabric makes it by absorbing light. The two ranges overlap but do not match, and they diverge most on exactly the colors teams find attractive.
rows: The widest gap of any hue. Screens produce violet at full red and blue intensity.
Deeper, calmer and slightly more blue. A good color, and not the one on the monitor.
Extremely vivid, because the eye is most sensitive in this part of the spectrum.
Slightly deeper and less electric. The most visible color on a court either way.
Unusually intense — a display carries most of its luminance in the green channel.
A step calmer in dye. The second-largest gap after purple.
Close to accurate, because both sit low on the luminance scale.
Reliable. These are the colors a screen misleads least about.
Bright, and with far less contrast against a number than the screen suggests.
blocks.close: The reliable route is a Pantone value or a physical garment rather than a screen color. Matching against fabric accounts for how the dye actually sits on that knit, which no image can convey — where screen and dyed color diverge covers the mechanism.

blocks.h3: Choosing a color that works on a court
items: Check the division first. Navy, black and red are the three most common colors in the sport, and being the fourth navy team costs you recognition you paid for.

Settle the number color before the jersey color. On a light base a dark number is required; on a dark one a light number is. Choosing the base first and the number second is how a set ends up illegible.
Judge the pair in grayscale. If the number and the ground go to similar shades, they will merge under gym lighting whatever the hues are.
Record the Pantone references and keep them with the program's records. Every future order then matches this one rather than approximating it.
Order the jersey and shorts together. The two fabrics take dye at different rates, so ordering them separately produces a top and a bottom that are a shade apart.

callout.p: Ordering "royal blue" or "green" as a word rather than a value. Both are ranges rather than colors, and two orders placed a year apart will land in different parts of the range — which is how a program ends up owning two blues and having to pick one.

colored-jerseys-uniforms.close: Color is also where a program can be distinctive for free. Green, purple and yellow are all under-used in amateur basketball, and in a division of navy and black teams any of them is identifiable from the parking lot. That recognition costs exactly the same as being the fourth navy team.

faqs.q: Why does the color look different from the screen?
faqs.a: Because a screen makes color by adding light and fabric makes it by absorbing light, and the two ranges do not fully overlap. Purple, orange and kelly green disagree most. Use a proof to judge layout and contrast, and a Pantone value or a physical sample to judge the color itself.

faqs.q: Can you match our existing kit?
faqs.a: Usually, and the way to do it is to send a physical garment rather than a photograph or a color name. Matching against the garment accounts for how the dye sits on that particular fabric. If the original was a different fabric type we will say honestly how close the match will get before you commit.

faqs.q: Which number color should we use?
faqs.a: Whichever has the most contrast with the base, judged as though the color were removed. White on navy, dark on yellow, gold on purple. What fails is a mid-toned number on a mid-toned base, which is the combination that looks richest in a design file.

faqs.q: How do we stop our color drifting between orders?
faqs.a: Record the Pantone references on the first order and keep them with the program rather than with a person. Every subsequent order then references a value rather than a memory, which is what stops a club ending up with two versions of its own blue.

faqs.q: Will the color fade?
faqs.a: Every dyed fabric fades. Orange, yellow and fluorescent colors fade fastest; navy and black slowest. A design dyed into the fiber fades with the garment rather than separating from it, so the set ages as one piece — and ordering spares with the main run keeps a mid-season addition from standing out.

custom-printed-jerseys.h2: The design goes inside the fabric, not on top of it
intro: Every other way of decorating a jersey adds a layer to it. Screen printing lays ink on the surface, twill stitches cloth onto it, vinyl bonds a film to it.
All of them work, and all of them share one eventual failure: the added layer and the fabric beneath it age at different rates, and after enough seasons the layer cracks, lifts or peels.

Printing the design into the fabric adds no layer at all. The dye converts to a gas under heat and bonds into the polyester fibers themselves, so what comes out is fabric that is a different color rather than fabric with something stuck to it.

items: More than three or four colors. Screen printing charges per color because each is a separate screen and pass. Printing charges nothing for color count, so a twelve-color design costs what a two-color one does.
Gradients, fades and photographic elements. Straightforward this way and effectively impossible with a screen.
Anything crossing a seam. The panels are printed flat and assembled afterwards, so a stripe can carry over the shoulder or around the ribs. No decoration applied to a finished garment can do that.
A set that has to last several seasons. Nothing on the surface means nothing to lift, and the design fades with the garment rather than separating from it.
Shorts especially. Floor abrasion sits exactly where an applied hip stripe would be, and a dyed one has nothing to abrade off.

callout.p: There is no white sublimation dye. The white in a printed jersey is the fabric showing through where nothing was printed, which means the process starts from white or very light fabric and the design supplies every color including the background. It is rarely a real constraint, because a design that would need it can nearly always be inverted — but it surprises people, and it is better said here than discovered at proof stage.

steps.p: A vector file, a photograph of last season's kit, or a description and two colors. We will tell you within a day which of those it is and what it needs.

steps.h: The design is laid out on the pattern pieces
steps.p: Not onto a rectangle — across the flat panels that will become the front, back and sides. This is the stage where anything crossing a seam is positioned.

Look at it for number contrast against whatever sits behind it, for anything meant to meet across a seam actually meeting, and for the colors being the ones specified rather than the ones that looked right on a monitor.

steps.h: Revise it as many times as you like
steps.p: Design and proofing are free and there is no limit. This matters more with printing than with any other method, because the transfer genuinely does not look like the finished garment.

steps.h: Approve, and it goes to production
steps.p: Nothing is printed before that point, and the specification is kept on file so a reorder next season matches this one rather than approximating it.

custom-printed-jerseys.close: Do not simplify a design before sending it. Teams routinely cut colors out of an idea to keep the price down and then discover that the color count was never the cost — what moves the price is quantity, fabric and garment count. If you want to see the options before talking to anyone, the builder with a live preview takes about five minutes and commits you to nothing.

faqs.q: Does a more complicated design cost more?
faqs.a: No. The whole design prints in one pass rather than one screen per color, so colors, gradients and panel styles do not change the price. What sets the price is the garment, the quantity and how many pieces are in the set.

faqs.q: Will the print crack or peel?
faqs.a: It cannot, because there is nothing on the surface to crack — the dye is inside the fiber. What it does is fade, at the same rate as the garment around it, so a three-year-old jersey looks like an old jersey rather than a jersey with a damaged number on it.

faqs.q: Can you print onto cotton?
faqs.a: No. The dye bonds to polyester specifically; on cotton it has nothing to attach to and washes out. That is not a limitation for basketball, where performance fabric is polyester for reasons unrelated to printing.

faqs.q: Can a design run across a seam?
faqs.a: Yes, and only this way. The panels are printed while flat and assembled afterwards, so a stripe or graphic can continue over the shoulder or around the side. Any decoration applied to a finished garment stops where the seam does.

faqs.q: Why does the proof matter more here?
faqs.a: Because the printed transfer does not look like the finished garment — the dye changes appearance as it converts, and the fabric's own texture affects how the color reads. Approving the artwork file alone would be approving something nobody has seen.

custom-uniforms.h2: Two garments that have to match, ordered as one
intro: A uniform is a jersey and a pair of shorts, and the single most common complaint about one is that the two halves are not quite the same color.

Not badly wrong — a shade apart, visible in photographs, obvious when twelve players stand together. It happens because the two were ordered as two things, from two fabrics that take dye at slightly different rates.

Ordering both on one job from one specification means they come off the same production run and are matched to each other rather than to a number. It costs nothing extra and it removes the complaint entirely.

blocks.h3: What a full set decision actually involves

rows.p: Basketball's home-and-away convention is lighter than football's, but a color clash still means somebody wears pinnies, and it is usually the visiting team. Ask how often that actually costs you something: two clashes a season is a pinnie problem, ten is a second-set problem.

Chest for the jersey and waist for the shorts. Players routinely take different sizes on top and below, and ordering both from a single letter guarantees returns on any roster above about ten. Together the two take about thirty seconds per player.

rows.h: The size run has to cover the roster you have
rows.p: A squad of twelve routinely spans a 32-inch chest and a 46-inch chest, and a guard and a center whose proportions differ in every dimension. That is why the inseam is cut proportionally within each size and the armhole drop moves with it, rather than one pattern scaled linearly.

A named jersey retires with the player whatever condition it is in; a numbered one goes to whoever needs it next season. For a program that reissues, names quietly convert a multi-season asset into a single-season one — which is why most settle on names for varsity and numbers below it.

rows.h: Spares, ordered with the main run
rows.p: Two or three in the middle sizes, unnamed, with numbers not already on the roster. Rosters move more than anyone plans for, and a spare bought now costs a fraction of a single-garment reorder in February.

items: Roster size and rough size spread. Enough for pricing within a business day; the precise measurements can follow.
Your two colors, as Pantone values or a physical garment rather than as words. This is the single biggest source of disappointment on a uniform order.
Any artwork that exists, in any state — a vector file, a photograph of last season's kit, a sketch. We will tell you within a day what it needs.
The date the kit must be in your hands, not the season. Everything is scheduled backwards from it.
Whether the set is being reissued, which changes the fabric, the names decision and the size spread all at once.

callout.cap: If the budget only stretches to one set
callout.p: Order the second set's specification anyway and have us hold it. Next year's shorts will then match this year's jersey exactly, rather than being matched to a garment that has already faded through a season.

custom-uniforms.close: Design and proofing are free, revisions are unlimited, and nothing is produced until you approve a proof. There is no minimum that would stop a normal team order — a twelve-player squad and a two-hundred-garment league order are both routine, and small orders simply cost more per garment because the setup is the same either way.

faqs.q: Why order the jersey and shorts together?
faqs.a: Because they are different fabrics and take dye at slightly different rates. Ordered on one job they come off the same production run and match each other; ordered separately they are each matched to a specification, and on a saturated color that produces a top and a bottom a shade apart.

faqs.q: Do we need home and away sets?
faqs.a: It depends on your schedule rather than on convention. If a color clash costs you something two or three times a season, a pinnie solves it and the money is better spent on the fabric of one good set. If it happens regularly, or you play tournaments on neutral floors, a second set is not a luxury.

faqs.q: How should we collect sizes?
faqs.a: Chest and waist on one form with one deadline, set a week earlier than you actually need it. Ask for measurements rather than size letters — a letter is a summary produced by whichever brand made the last garment somebody thought about.

faqs.q: Can players have different cuts in one set?
faqs.a: Yes, at no extra cost. The fabric, color, decoration and lettering are identical across every cut, so a mixed order reads as one uniform from the stands. Note the preference against each name on the roster sheet.

faqs.q: What is the timeline?
faqs.a: Production is predictable and we will give you a firm date. What varies is everything before it — collecting sizes, settling a design, getting artwork into a usable file, and approving a proof. Those are usually the longer half and they are the half you control.
